  • Why does my baby wake crying or screaming?
Newborn Care

Why does my baby wake crying or screaming?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Night waking can be loud and sudden, even after a peaceful stretch of sleep. Hunger, discomfort and ordinary development are common possibilities, but a cry is not a diagnosis. Check how your baby looks and responds first, then work through feeding, comfort and recent changes while keeping the sleep space safe.

Start with how your baby looks and responds

A sudden scream after quiet sleep can be alarming. Babies can stir, grunt, move and briefly cry between periods of sleep, but a cry alone cannot tell you whether the cause is hunger, discomfort, illness or a need for reassurance. The baby’s age, usual behaviour and accompanying symptoms matter more than how loudly they cry.

First look at breathing, colour, alertness and whether your baby responds normally. Get emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, a seizure, collapse or a baby who is unresponsive or unusually difficult to wake. Repeated forceful vomiting, a non-fading rash with illness or rapidly worsening distress also needs urgent medical attention. Do not spend time testing sleep strategies when your baby appears seriously unwell.

Hunger can interrupt sleep at any stage

Newborns need frequent feeds throughout the day and night, often every few hours and sometimes closer together. Longer sleep stretches develop at different rates. A baby who wakes after several hours may be hungry, but the right feeding plan depends on age, weight gain, milk transfer and any medical needs.

Respond to feeding cues and follow any advice about waking a young or vulnerable baby for feeds. Do not assume that reaching a certain age means night milk is no longer needed. If feeding seems ineffective, unusually tiring or persistently painful, ask a midwife, health visitor or feeding specialist to assess a feed.

Wind and feeding discomfort need context

A baby can swallow air during feeding or crying and may seem uncomfortable with trapped wind. Drawing the knees up, squirming or passing gas can occur, but none of these signs proves that gas is the only explanation for a distressed waking. Check the whole baby and consider the timing around feeds.

Gentle burping, a calm feeding pace and reviewing latch or bottle technique may help. Breast milk and standard infant formula are generally digestible for babies; ordinary crying is not evidence that the digestive system cannot handle many of their ingredients. Lactose intolerance is uncommon in infancy.

Cow’s-milk protein allergy and other feeding conditions need proper assessment. Repeated formula changes or removing foods from a breastfeeding parent’s diet should not be the default response to night crying. Cow’s milk as a main drink is also different from infant formula made with modified cow’s-milk ingredients. Seek advice if there is persistent vomiting, blood in the stool, poor growth or ongoing feeding distress.

Teething can be uncomfortable, but does not explain every fever

The first tooth often appears around six months, but some babies start much earlier or after their first birthday. Sore gums, increased drooling, chewing and a few unsettled nights can occur. Some teeth emerge with little discomfort. Months of repeated teething do not mean every night of severe crying has the same cause.

A clean finger gently massaging the gum or a suitable teething toy while awake may help. If medicine is needed, ask about an age- and weight-appropriate product and follow its directions. Do not give pain medicine simply to make a baby sleep.

Drooling or rubbing an ear does not confirm teething or an ear infection. A temperature of 38°C or higher, significant lethargy, poor feeding or persistent inconsolable crying should not be attributed to teething without considering illness.

Check the nappy, clothing and sleep environment

A wet or dirty nappy, damp clothing, a rough seam or a room that is uncomfortably warm or cool can disturb sleep. Check that the baby is dry and comfortably dressed, and replace soiled bedding. Keep lights and interaction calm where practical so care does not become an extended play session.

Comfort should stay compatible with safe sleep. Place the baby on their back on a firm, flat, non-inclined infant sleep surface with a fitted sheet. Keep pillows, loose blankets, soft toys and positioners out of the cot. Use appropriate sleep clothing rather than adding soft bedding to settle a baby, and avoid overheating.

Illness can first become noticeable at night

A blocked nose, fever, pain or another illness can wake a baby who had seemed comfortable earlier. If the baby feels hot, use a thermometer and note the reading. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs urgent medical assessment. At three to six months, 39°C or higher also requires prompt medical advice; lower temperatures do not make other worrying symptoms safe to ignore.

Contact a clinician for poor feeding, fewer wet nappies, persistent vomiting, unusual drowsiness or crying that is different from the baby’s usual pattern and cannot be settled. A very young baby may be seriously ill without a high fever. You do not need to identify the cause before asking for help.

Ear pulling, rubbing the face or settling briefly in your arms are observations to report, not diagnostic tests. If something feels wrong or symptoms are getting worse, seek assessment rather than waiting for the next scheduled feed or until morning.

Separation anxiety can increase the need for reassurance

During the second half of the first year, some babies become more aware of a parent’s absence and wake calling for them. This is a common developmental experience, not evidence that the child is manipulative or has done something wrong. Familiar voices, calm reassurance and a predictable response can help.

A baby who settles when you enter the room may have needed your presence, but this does not rule out hunger, pain or illness. There is no nine-month dividing line after which waking is mainly emotional. Older babies continue to have physical needs, and younger babies also need connection and comfort.

Sleep regressions are descriptions, not a compulsory timetable

Families often use sleep regression to mean that a baby who had slept for longer stretches has begun waking more often. Sleep can change with developing skills, altered naps, travel, illness, feeding needs or a different routine. The term does not identify one medical diagnosis or one cause.

Some changes are noticed around commonly discussed ages, but every child does not have to pass through regressions at four, six, eight, twelve, eighteen and twenty-four months. A calendar cannot confirm why a particular baby is waking. Look at what changed and how the baby is doing during the day as well as at night.

Familiar settling habits may matter without being a fault

A baby accustomed to falling asleep while feeding, rocking or hearing a familiar voice may seek the same conditions after waking. This can be tiring for caregivers, but it does not mean responsive care has damaged the baby’s sleep or that every waking is a learned problem.

If you want to change the pattern, start with a calm, repeatable routine and small adjustments that fit your baby’s development and feeding needs. A dummy or pacifier is optional; do not force it or attach it to clothing or a cord during sleep. If it falls out after the baby is asleep, it does not have to be replaced.

Appetite can change during growth

Some babies ask for milk more frequently during periods of rapid growth or change. A few hungrier nights can be temporary, and feeding responsively may help. The need for extra feeds should be understood alongside weight gain and how effectively the baby is feeding.

There is no reliable rule that every growth spurt lasts exactly two or three days. Nor does settling after milk prove that growth is the only cause. If the baby remains unusually hungry, feeds poorly, has fewer wet nappies or is not gaining as expected, request a feeding and health assessment.

Nightmares and night terrors are different experiences

A nightmare wakes a child from a frightening dream, often later in the night; an older child may remember it and seek comfort. During a night terror, the child may shout, scream or move while not fully awake and usually has no memory of it afterward. Night terrors are most common in children aged three to eight.

A young infant’s sudden cry does not establish that either event occurred, and there is no exact eighteen-month boundary that diagnoses the cause. Repeated unusual episodes, abnormal movements, breathing changes or a child who is unwell should be discussed with a clinician. A calm description of when the episode happens and what you observe can help distinguish possible explanations.

Use a short, responsive settling sequence

After checking for warning signs, work through feeding, a clean nappy, comfortable clothing and gentle reassurance. Try holding, a quiet voice or slow rocking while you remain awake. If a strategy makes the baby more alert or upset, simplify rather than adding more stimulation. Some babies need time and repeated calm support; there is no method that always reveals the cause immediately.

If you swaddle, place the baby only on their back, allow free hip movement and stop as soon as there are signs of trying to roll. Do not use a weighted swaddle, blanket or sleep sack. Swaddling is optional and does not reduce the risk of sudden infant death.

Return the baby to their own safe sleep space after comforting or feeding. Avoid falling asleep with a baby on a sofa or armchair. If another adult is available, agree on shifts or a handover before exhaustion makes it hard to stay awake.

Sleep training is a choice, not an unavoidable next step

Structured sleep approaches differ, and families make different choices about them. They are not a substitute for assessing pain, feeding or illness, and a newborn is not expected to manage without needed overnight care. A health professional can help you decide whether any particular approach fits the baby’s age, growth and medical situation.

There is no rule that two weeks of difficult nights makes formal sleep training mandatory, or that every habit is made or broken in fourteen days. Responsive settling and gradual changes remain options. If the current arrangement is no longer manageable, ask for practical support without feeling that you must use a method that conflicts with your family’s needs.

Make room for follow-up and caregiver support

Record the timing of wakes, feeds, nappies, any temperature and what helped, if doing so is manageable. Seek advice for recurrent unexplained distress, persistent sleep disruption or concern about growth. You can ask for help even if the baby has no obvious fever and even if another person thinks the waking is normal.

If crying is overwhelming, place the baby safely on their back in the cot and step away briefly to regain calm, checking back and asking another adult for help when possible. Never shake a baby. If you fear you might hurt yourself or the baby, seek immediate support.

Night waking often changes as babies develop, but parents also need rest and care now. Tell your healthcare team if exhaustion, anxiety or low mood is affecting your ability to cope. Support is appropriate without proving that the baby has a sleep disorder.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Sleep patterns and feeding needs change at different rates; a fixed regression calendar does not identify the cause of waking.

Age-specific fever thresholds and changes in breathing, alertness, intake or hydration take priority over settling strategies.

How BeMama can help

Keep a simple record of wakes and symptoms if useful, and agree on a realistic overnight handover with another caregiver.

When to seek help

Seek urgent assessment for fever in a young baby, poor feeding or unusual persistent distress. Breathing difficulty, abnormal colour, seizures or a baby who is hard to wake needs emergency help. Never shake a baby.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Start with breathing, colour, alertness and signs of illness.
  • Hunger and physical discomfort remain possible in older babies.
  • Settling when held does not rule out a medical problem.
  • Neither regressions nor growth spurts follow one compulsory calendar.
  • Safe sleep and support for exhausted caregivers remain essential.

Frequently asked questions

Does a sudden scream tell me what is wrong?

No. Consider the baby’s age, usual behaviour, feeding and other symptoms. Check for illness before assuming the cause is a sleep habit.

When does fever need urgent assessment?

Under three months, 38°C or higher requires urgent medical assessment. At three to six months, 39°C or higher needs prompt advice. Concerning symptoms at any temperature still matter.

If my baby calms when I arrive, can I rule out illness?

No. Comfort can help a baby who is hungry or unwell as well as one experiencing separation anxiety. The response is not a diagnostic test.

Is breast milk or formula too difficult for babies to digest?

Usually not. Wind and crying have many explanations, and lactose intolerance is uncommon in babies. Seek feeding advice before making repeated formula or diet changes.

Can teething explain a temperature of 38°C or more?

Do not assume that it does. Teething may cause sore gums and mild unsettledness, but fever or marked illness needs age-appropriate assessment.

Will every baby have a four-month or eight-month regression?

No. These are common descriptions of possible changes, not compulsory stages or a diagnosis for every difficult night.

Must a growth spurt end after three days?

No. There is no fixed duration. Ongoing feeding concerns, reduced wet nappies or poor growth deserve assessment rather than being labelled a long growth spurt.

Does night crying mean my infant has nightmares?

Not necessarily. Nightmares and night terrors are different and are easier to recognise in older children. Repeated unusual episodes should be discussed with a clinician.

Is formal sleep training necessary after two difficult weeks?

No. There is no two-week rule. Feeding and health needs come first, and families can choose responsive or gradual approaches with support.

What if I feel overwhelmed by the crying?

Put the baby safely on their back in their cot, take a brief calming break and ask for help. Never shake the baby, and seek immediate support if you fear anyone may be harmed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
